plan.question: Could a people's voice override the state?

chapters.title: The Orange Tide
beats: Ukraine stood at a crossroads between East and West, with two rival camps facing off in a presidential election.
Mass protests erupted in the capital, pitting citizens against the state apparatus in a bid to reverse a fraudulent vote.
This confrontation established a new geopolitical alignment and precipitated deep friction with neighboring powers, raising the stakes for the region's future.
chapters.hook: How did a nation's voice break the machinery of power?

chapters.title: The Rivals
beats: Viktor Yushchenko, the opposition leader, sought to steer Ukraine toward the West, relying on his moral authority and the support of his ally Yulia Tymoshenko.
Leonid Kuchma, the incumbent president, aimed to preserve the existing power structure and his own influence, overseeing the state's response to the crisis.
Viktor Yanukovych, the prime minister, represented the pro-government camp and the interests of the Party of Regions, backed by significant financial support from Moscow.
Vladimir Putin, Russia's president, viewed Ukraine as a crucial sphere of influence, with his administration actively supporting Yanukovych's bid for the presidency.
The stage was set in Kyiv, the capital where the political heart of the nation beat, and Maidan Nezalezhnosti, the central square that would become the soul of the protest.

chapters.title: Poison and Polls
beats: In September 2004, Viktor Yushchenko suffered severe dioxin poisoning under mysterious circumstances, an event that galvanized public sympathy and intensified scrutiny of the election process.

In the spring of 2004, opposition activists traveled to Novi Sad, Serbia, to meet with leaders of the group that led civic opposition to Milošević, who taught Ukrainian youth how to control the temperature of protesting crowds.
The first round of the presidential election was held on 31 October 2004, resulting in a narrow margin with Yushchenko receiving 39.87% of the vote and Viktor Yanukovych receiving 39.32%.
Yulia Tymoshenko and Viktor Yushchenko had already established the Force of the People coalition, agreeing on Tymoshenko's future nomination as prime minister to strengthen their united front.

chapters.title: The Runoff
beats: On 21 November 2004, the runoff election took place, but the Yushchenko campaign called for mass protests following exit polls and allegations of widespread fraud.
President Leonid Kuchma and Prime Minister Viktor Yanukovych maintained that the election was legitimate, with the pro-government camp confident in their hold on the state machinery.
By 24 November 2004, negotiations between Viktor Yushchenko and President Leonid Kuchma collapsed, and the Central Election Commission officially certified Yanukovych as the winner.
The decision to certify the result despite mounting evidence of irregularities set the stage for a direct confrontation between the state and the people.

chapters.title: The Court's Verdict
beats: On 3 December 2004, the Supreme Court of Ukraine convened to review the presidential runoff results.
The justices listened to arguments from both sides, weighing the evidence of fraud against the official certification by the Central Election Commission.
In a decisive ruling, the Supreme Court invalidated the fraudulent runoff results and ordered a re-vote to be held on 26 December 2004.
This legal victory for the opposition marked the turning point, shifting the balance of power from the executive branch to the will of the people as expressed through the courts.

chapters.title: Orange Sea
beats: Massive protests began across Ukraine on 22 November 2004, with organizations undertaking the management of demonstrations in Kyiv.
On 23 November 2004, an estimated 500,000 protesters peacefully marched in front of the Verkhovna Rada building, wearing orange to symbolize their support for Yushchenko.
Viktor Yushchenko addressed supporters in Kyiv, urging nationwide mass protests, general strikes, and sit-ins to force the government to concede defeat.
On 28 November 2004, over 10,000 internal ministry troops were mobilized to put down the protests, but they were pulled back after interventions by Ukrainian security and intelligence chiefs.

On 1 December 2004, the Verkhovna Rada condemned federalization actions and passed a non-confidence vote in Prime Minister Viktor Yanukovych's cabinet, further isolating the pro-government leadership.
chapters.hook: Could the state crush the people, or would the people reshape the state?

chapters.title: The New President
beats: The repeat presidential runoff election was conducted on 26 December 2004 under domestic and international observation.
On 10 January 2005, the Central Election Commission officially declared Viktor Yushchenko the winner of the presidential election after dismissing Yanukovych's legal challenges.
Viktor Yushchenko was officially inaugurated as President of Ukraine on 23 January 2005, bringing the Orange Revolution to an end.
In 2006, the 2004 constitutional amendments shifting power from the presidency to parliament came into effect, enabling Viktor Yanukovych to return as Prime Minister heading a coalition.

In 2010, Viktor Yanukovych won the presidential election against Yulia Tymoshenko, succeeding Viktor Yushchenko, and the Constitutional Court of Ukraine overturned the 2004 constitutional amendments on 1 October 2010, declaring them unconstitutional.
